items.text: Conductor count written down first — including the equipment ground — and the Table 1 percentage picked from that count (53% one, 31% two, 40% three or more, 60% nipple 24 in or less).
Table 4 row matches the raceway actually being installed (EMT is not PVC Schedule 40 at the same trade size).
Every conductor's area taken from Table 5 for its actual insulation type; bare conductors taken from Table 8.
Same-size pulls divided; mixed-size pulls added line by line. Result rounded down, except the all-same-size 0.8 round-up.
Voltage drop run with the actual load current and the round-trip factor (2 single-phase, 1.732 three-phase as an approximation), using the stranded/solid and metal row that matches the conductor.
Voltage-drop result compared with the 3% branch / 5% feeder-plus-branch figures and written up as a recommendation, not a code requirement; any stricter limit traced to the project spec or AHJ.
If a voltage-drop result is close to a limit, or the run is a large three-phase feeder, flag it for a Table 9 check instead of settling it with the Table 8 approximation.
CCA run? The Table 8 aluminum column was used only as a labeled approximation — no CCA resistance invented.
CCA sizing, where the lead has picked CCA: one AWG larger per S-10, terminations listed for the conductor, never backstabbed.
Commercial branch circuit in the example or the run: started at Sharma's 20A / 12 AWG copper minimum per S-01 before any voltage-drop upsize — company practice, not a Chapter 9 requirement.

Material stated before the math — copper, aluminum, or CCA named on the calculation; CCA sized from the Table 310.16 aluminum column, fill run at the (possibly upsized) AWG, and voltage drop for CCA run on the Table 8 aluminum column as a labeled approximation (no CCA resistance value invented)
